items.question: How do I convert an annual salary to an hourly rate?
items.answer: Divide annual gross salary by the annual hours you assume. At 40 hours per week for 52 weeks, $62,400 / 2,080 = $30 per hour. This is gross pay, not take-home pay. In this model, non-hourly inputs are interpreted as adjusted pay; set time-off days to zero for the simple 52-week comparison. Paid leave should not automatically be subtracted as lost earnings.

Neither tool predicts overtime eligibility or your employer’s exact payroll withholding.

items.question: What are FICA and OASDI on my paycheck?
items.answer: FICA is the federal payroll-tax framework that includes Social Security and Medicare taxes. OASDI refers to the Social Security portion, not an extra tax to add on top of Social Security. Review the Social Security and Medicare rows in this result rather than subtracting FICA and OASDI twice. Individual payroll deductions and covered wages can differ.

items.question: Why does this estimate differ from my actual paycheck?
items.answer: This tool estimates annual tax liability and allocates it across equal pay periods. It does not reproduce the IRS Publication 15-T withholding calculation from your Form W-4. State and local taxes use effective rates you enter, not a complete jurisdiction-specific engine. Bonuses, changing wages, benefit treatment and employer rounding can also differ. Compare the result with your pay statement and official withholding resources.

items.question: Why do biweekly and semimonthly paychecks differ?
items.answer: No. This model uses 26 equal pay periods for biweekly pay and 24 for semimonthly pay. With the same annual modeled take-home amount, dividing by 26 yields a smaller payment than dividing by 24. Real payroll calendars can have a different count in some years; use the arrangement that matches the scenario and do not treat this as a dated payroll calendar.

items.question: How long will it take to pay off my credit card?
items.answer: For a single fixed-rate balance, choose Fixed Monthly Payment and enter the total amount you plan to pay. On the illustrative $6,000 balance at 20% APR, $200 per month takes 42 payments; $300 takes 25. Interest falls from $2,386.99 to $1,359.64. These monthly-accrual examples assume no new charges, fees or rate changes; they are not your issuer’s daily statement calculation.

items.question: How much rent can I afford at $18 or $22 per hour?
items.answer: First choose your work-hours assumption. At 40 paid hours per week for 52 weeks, gross annual pay is $37,440 at $18/hour and $45,760 at $22/hour. With no monthly debt, a 30% rent ratio and 36% total-debt ratio, the model gives $936 and $1,144 monthly. These are illustrative planning ceilings, not a landlord’s approval or a guarantee that the remaining budget covers living costs.

items.question: Does this calculate gross margin or net profit margin?
items.answer: The business modes calculate (revenue minus entered cost) divided by revenue. When cost is the cost of goods sold, that is gross margin. Net profit requires all applicable expenses and taxes; it is not automatically computed from a product-cost input. Keep stock and currency collateral modes separate from business profit percentages.

items.question: How are gross margin and markup different?
items.answer: Both use the same dollar difference, but margin divides it by selling price and markup divides it by cost. Cost $100 and selling price $150 give $50 profit, 50% markup and 33.3333% gross margin. A 30% markup is not a 30% margin. Use Markup Calculator to convert percentages or solve a selling price from either target.

how to calculate markup percentage
items.question: How do I calculate selling price using markup?
items.answer: Use selling price = cost × (1 + markup/100). With $100 cost and 30% markup, price is $130 and profit is $30. Gross margin is 30/130 = 23.0769%, because it uses selling price as the denominator. Do not subtract 30% from the selling price to reverse a 30% markup; divide by 1.30 instead.

queries: how to calculate markup from margin

items.question: How do I convert markup to margin, or margin to markup?
items.answer: Margin as a decimal = markup / (1 + markup). Markup = margin / (1 − margin). Enter percentages in the form: 50% markup corresponds to 33.3333% margin, while a 30% margin requires about 42.8571% markup. These conversions do not include sales tax, overhead or channel fees unless already accounted for in the stated cost model.
